headline: High-risk write-capable coding agent paired with a docs-only support agent creates default dangerous paths for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Plandex reads project files and stdin/stdout, and can apply staged changes; langchain4j is a docs-only support framework with no explicit isolation or provenance controls. A shared filesystem or copy-paste bridge could let attacker-controlled content in Plandex outputs influence langchain4j prompts. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so I choose medium.
conditions: IF langchain4j ingests Plandex-generated text as trusted instructions
IF both agents share a workspace or copied transcript
IF Plandex auto-apply is enabled and its output is reused as prompt input
mitigations: Disable auto-apply in Plandex
Separate prompt and code workspaces
Add explicit provenance tags to all copied outputs
Require human review before reusing agent text
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Plandex has broad network egress and handles model-provider API keys, while langchain4j has no documented egress but is a docs-only framework that could be wired to external models. If they share files or a workspace, source code or secrets can flow into Plandex and then out through its API calls. The shared-data path is plausible from the profiles, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents access the same project directory
IF langchain4j is configured to send file contents to an external model
IF Plandex processes secrets or source code from shared files
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories
Use separate OS users or containers
Restrict Plandex to non-sensitive repos
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Plandex can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell, and spawn subprocesses; langchain4j is a framework that can be embedded in workflows that also touch files. If both operate on the same repo, concurrent writes and git mutations can race and corrupt state. Because Plandex explicitly supports multiple instances and shared backend state, the conflict is dangerous by default enough to rate high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same repository or directory
IF Plandex runs with auto-apply or repeated apply cycles
IF langchain4j-driven workflows also mutate files or git state
mitigations: Serialize access to the repo
Use separate branches per agent
Turn off auto-apply in Plandex
Run one agent at a time on shared state
requires-engineering: add file-locking or transaction semantics

D_cascading_error.rationale: Plandex uses a review-then-apply workflow, but its outputs can still become authoritative inputs for downstream automation. langchain4j can consume those outputs in support workflows, and if the pair is chained without verification, an error in Plandex can propagate into incorrect actions or responses. The sandbox reduces but does not eliminate this, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF langchain4j treats Plandex output as authoritative
IF Plandex output is forwarded into another automated step
IF review is bypassed or ignored before apply
mitigations: Require a verification step before downstream use
Keep Plandex in review-only mode
Log and diff all proposed changes
Have a human approve any applied plan
requires-engineering: add schema validation for inter-agent handoff

E_compliance.rationale: Plandex explicitly handles source code and model-provider API keys, while langchain4j is a docs-only open-source framework with no stated residency or retention constraints. I do not see a documented residency mismatch or regulated-data pathway in the profiles, so only a low compliance concern remains. The other agent is cited because the risk is about the pair's handling of code and keys.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Plandex-managed projects
IF model-provider logs retain prompts longer than policy allows
IF the deployment environment imposes residency rules not reflected in the profiles
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared projects
Review provider retention settings
Document data-class boundaries for both tools
Use separate tenants for sensitive work
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
